![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/3c08141f91eea5b2d2006926de5239f91630de139fae970147d8267d46429392.png)

Consider the RCL circuit shown above. Given that the current $I(t)$ in the circuit at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t}+\frac{P}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{Q}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),
$$

where $A,$ $B,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
question.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=6I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 60\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+2I=30\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+2{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+3(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\,\, \\ +2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =30\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ (-7\alpha +9\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-9\alpha -7\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =30\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-7\alpha +9\beta =30\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -9\alpha -7\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{21}{13}$ and $\beta =\frac{27}{13}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{21}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{27}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t}-\frac{21}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{27}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=-21$ and $Q=27,$ and

$$
P+Q=-21+27=6.
$$
